name: Liam Usman

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for joining, Liam. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. What you say is confidential, so feel free to say what you'd say in public and what you really think. How does a normal working day go for you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I buy phone cases, chargers, cables and earbuds for Voltline Distribution, which supplies electronics shops and supermarkets. I start by asking my AI assistant to summarise overnight sales and flag anything odd, then I spend the morning on calls with factories and agents. Callum, the head of category, sets the margin targets and I'm still the junior on the team after two and a half years. Honestly I love it when a supplier slips a price and I catch it with a tool before anyone else does.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My partner Hana teaches Year 4 at a primary school, we've got Zayn, nine, and Mina, six, and a house in Kingsmead with a mortgage we can handle. We have over six months of savings plus a bit in an index fund. I coach Zayn's football team on Saturdays, which is the best bit of my week.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say fair enough, it's a good tool and a bad religion. At work I'd say let's keep using it where it saves time, and I'd show Priyanka, my teammate, the tricks. To friends I'd say it's like spreadsheets in the nineties, useful and not magic.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, it barely changes my life. I'm already getting a few hours back a week and that's the plateau, a few hours. The job still needs someone who rings the factory and says the last batch of cables was rubbish.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on and keep tinkering. I'd try to build a little script that checks every price list against the last one, because that's the sort of thing I'd do on a Sunday afternoon. I'd keep saving about 300 a month into the index fund.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, a bit bored perhaps. If nothing changes, I'm in a decent job with a decent wage and a decent cushion.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You use AI every day. What would it mean if it turned out mostly hype?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If it was hype, my edge over people who don't use it shrinks. But that's fine, I'd still be quicker than most of them. I just wouldn't get the head start I thought I had.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does being the junior bother you at all?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not much, because I'm on the same wage ladder as everyone. I'd like the senior role in three or four years, and tools help me look good. If the tools are overrated I'd still have Callum's trust and some hard facts on my side.

say: I'd say it's a good tool and a bad **religion**, much like spreadsheets in the nineties.
At work I'd show my teammate Priyanka the **tricks**.
think: It barely changes my life, because the job still needs someone who rings the **factory** and complains.
If it's hype, my head start over people who don't use AI **shrinks**.
do: Build a little **script** that checks each new price list against the last one.
Keep saving **300** a month into the index fund.
Keep showing teammates which tasks the tool really **speeds** up.
feel: **Calm**, maybe a bit bored, in a decent job with a decent cushion.
S0.quote: I'd say fair enough, it's a good tool and a bad religion.
fieldNote: Already uses AI daily, so a quiet world costs him a head start, not a job.
Treats tools as a **hobby** as well as work.
Secure money and a wide local job market keep him calm.

steps.text: Write a script to compare each new price list with the last
Save 300 a month into the index fund
Keep buying and showing teammates the useful AI tricks

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's real now, not a fad, and it's going to speed up buying a lot. At work I'd say let's own it ourselves, so we're the people who shape how it runs. Online I'd post about what works and what doesn't, because I'd rather people see real examples than panic.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, a chunk of buying is going to be automatic: the reordering, the price checks, the supplier emails. I'm the junior, so the first things to go are my kind of tasks. The upside is I'm the junior who understands the tools, and that might keep me ahead of the senior who doesn't.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd put myself forward to run the AI buying pilot at Voltline, in writing, to Callum. I'd start learning basic data skills, like SQL, through the free course I've been eyeing. And I'd build a small side thing, perhaps a price-tracking sheet for the independent shops we supply.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy but fired up. It could be good or bad, and what decides it is whether I'm one of the people steering it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which parts of your own day would the tools take first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The routine reorders, the comparing of quotes, the first draft of every email. What stays is who we trust, what a factory's word is worth and the odd emergency, like a ship stuck in a port.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do if Callum asked you to train the older buyers?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say yes in a second, and I'd be honest. Some of them will take to it, some won't, and I'd tell them the dull parts will go and the judgement part gets more valuable. I'd just hope the firm doesn't use the training as a way to pick who to let go.

Online I'd post what works and what doesn't so people see **real** examples.

As the junior who understands the tools, I might stay **ahead** of seniors who don't.

Start learning **SQL** through a free course.
Build a price-tracking sheet for the independent **shops** we supply.
feel: **Uneasy** but fired up, because it comes down to whether I'm steering it.
S1.quote: The dull parts will go and the judgement part gets more valuable.
fieldNote: Treats the disruption as a chance to steer it, but knows junior tasks go first.
Moves toward **data skills** and a side tool, matching his adaptive profile.

steps.text: Offer in writing to run the AI buying pilot at Voltline
Learn SQL through a free online course
Build a price-tracking sheet for independent shops

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we'll need strong safety nets and fast. At work I'd say the buying team has about a year before things change a lot, so let's get our skills ready. To friends and online I'd say this is the moment to push for a basic income pilot and retraining paid for by the companies making the gains.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, my desk job is gone. AGI does buying better than I do, so the 2028 date is also the date my work becomes something a machine does. The comfort is that Voltline's warehouse still needs people until about 2031, and Hana's teaching is quite human work, so we're not both hit at once.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd use the first year to build something of my own, a small online business or consulting for shops that want to use AI for buying. I'd cut the spending we don't need, mainly takeaways and subscriptions, and I'd save 600 a month instead of 300. I'd also start talking to a financial adviser, because I'd be changing how we earn.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, honestly. I'm excited by the technology, but two years is short for a family with a mortgage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You like tools. Is full AGI something you'd welcome or fear?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Welcome it as a tool, fear it as an employer. I'd love the thing, I just don't love the bit where my boss can swap me for it. If I own a shop that sells buying help, I'm on the right side of it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens to Hana's job and to your kids' schooling?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Hana's school will keep going, though budgets might wobble if taxes drop. I'd tell Zayn to keep being curious and learn to make things, and I'd tell Mina the same once she's older. I'd also say don't wait for school to teach you the tools.

say: I'd say we need strong safety nets and **fast**, and companies making the gains should pay for retraining.
I'd push online for a basic **income** pilot.
think: My desk job is **gone** by 2028, because AGI buys better than I do.
The warehouse needs people until about **2031** and Hana's teaching is human work, so we're not both hit at once.
do: Build a small online **business** or consulting practice for shops that want AI buying help.
Cut takeaways and subscriptions and save **600** a month instead of 300.

feel: **Anxious**, because I'm excited by the technology but two years is short for a family with a mortgage.
S2.quote: I'd love the thing, I just don't love the bit where my boss can swap me for it.
fieldNote: Enthusiasm for the tech sits beside real fear for his own desk job.
Knows the three-year gap between thinking AI and robots helps his household because Hana's job is human work.
Reacts by building something **of his own**.

steps.text: Launch a small consulting service helping shops buy with AI
Book a session with a financial adviser

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is a fair warning, so let's use it. At work I'd ask management to start a skills plan for buyers now. I'd tell friends to try the tools weekly, just to know what they can and can't do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think it's still the same ending for my desk, but five years lets me make a real move. Seeing it coming is half the battle, and I'd rather be a few steps ahead of the layoffs than behind them. I'd feel about as safe as anyone with a mortgage and a bit of cash.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In year one I'd move toward a hybrid role at Voltline, part buying, part tool owner. I'd put away about 450 a month and keep the index fund going. I'd also try one or two projects on the side, like a price-comparison tool for shops, to see if it could grow.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. It's a good level of uneasy, the sort that gets you moving rather than freezing you.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does five years change the picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stay as long as they treat me well and teach me things. If a better offer came from a company that's more AI-first, I'd take it, and I wouldn't feel guilty. Loyalty is nice but my family eats first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you still stay at Voltline?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the difference is whether I get to the next step before everyone else does. Two years I'm sprinting and a bit scared, five years I'm walking quickly and thinking. I'd rather plan than panic.

S3.quote: Two years I'm sprinting and a bit scared, five years I'm walking quickly and thinking.

steps.text: Ask Callum for a hybrid buyer and tool owner role
Save 450 a month and keep the index fund going

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a long runway and everyone should be using it. At work I'd say don't wait for a crisis, build your skills now. To friends I'd say we should push for policies that share the gains and avoid a rush at the end.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'd be fine. I'd be fifty-three, the mortgage mostly gone, the kids nearly grown, and I'd have had ten years to build something or find a role where a person still matters. I'd still expect my current buying job to go, but I'd see it coming from a long way off.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep the day job and slowly grow the side thing, and invest more in the index fund. I'd learn things for fun, like data analysis and a bit of coding. Maybe by year five I'd have moved into a role that manages systems rather than buys by hand.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Quite good, actually. I'd feel I had room to play.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Ten years. Do you slow down?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit, but not much. I'd still use the tools every day, I just wouldn't push to be the first one to pilot everything. I'd do more with Zayn's football team, honestly, because the time is going.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you want your kids to know about work by then?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That the person who can ask a good question will beat the person who knows lots of answers. That being kind and being curious will matter more than being the best at one task. And that it's fine to change jobs more than once.

I'd push for policies that **share** the gains.
think: I'd be fine: 53, mortgage mostly gone, and a **decade** to find a role where a person still matters.
I'd still expect my current buying job to go but see it coming from **far** off.

feel: Quite **good**, actually, with room to play.
S4.quote: The person who can ask a good question will beat the person who knows lots of answers.
fieldNote: A decade removes most of the threat for someone who already uses AI daily.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, because there isn't time. I'd be building my own thing fast while Voltline decides what to do with me. What would help is a proper safety net, like paid retraining and some income cover while you switch, and an employer who tells you the plan early.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Just that I'm not afraid of the tech, I'm afraid of the timing. If it comes slowly, I think it's the best thing to happen to buying. I just want everyone to get the same head start I got.

headlineQuote: I'm not afraid of the tech, I'm afraid of the timing.
portrait: Liam is a **43-year-old** junior buyer at Voltline Distribution, covering phone accessories, chargers and cables for electronics shops.
He uses AI **every day**, loves experimenting with tools, and treats them as both his job and his hobby.
He has a mortgage, two children, Hana's teaching salary and over six months of savings plus an index fund.
He expects his buying desk to go in the AGI worlds, but plans to **build** something of his own.
He feels **calm** with no change or a slow one, and anxious only when the warning is two years.
biggestWorry: The **two-year** picture worries him most because it leaves no time to build a new income.
whatWouldHelp: Paid **retraining**, income cover while switching, and an employer who shares the plan early.
